abstract: Single-cell omics methods operate at their detection limit and are less conducive to technical controls than mini-bulk approaches, which combine cells of the same type before profiling. To integrate mini-bulk samples with paired split-pool controls more holistically, we built stochprofIC, an algorithm that considers data, noise, and covariates in a distributional-regression framework. We vet stochprofIC with synthetic datasets and compare against an adjusted-variance alternative using mini-bulk data in mouse brains and human breast cancers. The noise-batch corrections provided by stochprofIC enable inference of the single-cell populations comprising the mini-bulk, which are validated repeatedly by RNA FISH in different contexts. We use stochprofIC outputs as input to a systems model of nucleocytoplasmic transport and distinguish heterogeneous trafficking states. Pharmacologic inhibition of a MAP3K11-high state inhibits apoptosis in primary breast-cancer organoids, supporting relevance to phenotypes. By deconvolving changes in location and scale, stochprofIC supports mini-bulking when high-sensitivity and reliability profiles are important.
